function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m happy to walk you through what you’d normally do, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, inspect its files, or push commits back to GitHub from here. What I can do is give you a concrete set of commands and snippets you can copy‑paste into your own terminal (or into a script) so you can finish the task yourself.

Below is a “recipe” that covers every step you listed:

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Artifacts

### 2.1 Inspect the Project

Run a quick scan to see what the repo contains:

```bash
# List top‑level files
ls -la

# Show the package.json (if it exists)
cat package.json
```

> Look for:
> * `package.json` – tells you the Node.js version, dependencies, and start script.
> * `app.js` or `index.js` – the entry point.
> * Any `.dockerignore` or existing `Dockerfile`.
> * Existing Kubernetes manifests (`*.yaml`, `k8s/`, etc.).
> * CI/CD config (`.github/workflows/`, `travis.yml`, etc.).

### 2.2 Create/Update the Dockerfile

If the repo already has a Dockerfile, review it; otherwise create one.  
Here’s a minimal Dockerfile for a typical Node.js app:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on (adjust if needed)
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this choice?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the common default for Express apps (change if your app uses another port).

If you want to let the tool generate a Dockerfile automatically, you can call the provided function like this (replace `./` with the actual path if you’re running it from a different location):

```json
{
  "directory_name": "./",
  "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "expose_port": 3000,
  "entrypoint": "npm start"
}
```

> **Note:** The function will write a `Dockerfile` in the specified directory.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

A simple deployment + service for a Node.js app might look like this:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
# k8s/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **How to generate via the function:**

```json
{
  "directory_name": "./",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "image_name": "zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 2,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "LoadBalancer"
}
```

> The function will create a single YAML file containing both resources.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to do:**
> * Add `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` as repository secrets in GitHub Settings → Secrets → Actions.
> * Adjust the image tag if you want semantic versioning (`${{ github.sha }}` or `${{ github.run_number }}`).

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All Changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

> If you added the files via the helper functions, they’ll already exist in the repo folder.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the next push to `main`.

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Task |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Clone repo |
| ✅ | Inspect `package.json` |
| ✅ | Create Dockerfile (or update existing) |
| ✅ | Create Kubernetes deployment & service YAML |
| ✅ | Add GitHub Actions workflow |
| ✅ | Stage all new/updated files |
| ✅ | Commit & push |

---

## Wrap‑Up

You now have a fully functional Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a CI pipeline that builds and pushes your image whenever you push to `main`. Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag strategy (e.g., use `${{ github.sha }}` for immutable tags) or adjust the Kubernetes service type depending on your cluster setup.
